title: Comments, constants, and literals: meaning instead of magic numbers
goal: Separate a human explanation from a value used by the program.

prerequisites.text: You know declarations, an integer literal and output.

sections.title: From the task to an operation
paragraphs: // starts a comment lasting to the end of the line: it is not an executable statement. const int days = 7 creates an integer that cannot be reassigned through this name. 7 is an integer literal; "days" is a string literal, just output text.

A named constant avoids repeating an unexplained number, but a comment should describe the reason, such as counting whole weeks. Changing a comment does not change the calculation. constexpr suits a value computed at compile time; const alone does not promise compile-time evaluation in every case.

sections.title: Separate a human explanation from a value used by the program.
trace: Declared the fixed length of a week.
The number of weeks is separate data.
The comment does not change the state.
Multiplied values, not the comment text.

sections.title: Change one condition and check the prediction
paragraphs: Change only the comment. Then change weeks from 2 to 3.
Changing the comment leaves output at 14.

sections.title: When the result differs
paragraphs: Assigning daysPerWeek=8 after declaration is invalid; writing “now 8” in a comment does not change 7 either.

sections.title: Now solve your own task
paragraphs: Declare const int minutesPerHour=60 and calculate minutes in three hours. Add a comment explaining the number.
Practice contains a separate starter. Predict the result before changing your program. Returning to the example does not replace your source.

selfcheck.prompt: What output follows the specified change? Change only the comment. Then change weeks from 2 to 3.
selfcheck.feedback: Changing the comment leaves output at 14. Three whole weeks are 7×3=21 days.

selfcheck.prompt: Declare const int minutesPerHour=60 and calculate minutes in three hours. Add a comment explaining the number.
selfcheck.feedback: Compare the output with the readable reference case below. Explain each change using the objects or operations in this topic. minutesPerHour stays 60 and hours=3 produces 180. Assigning minutesPerHour=30 after its const declaration is invalid; a comment does not change its value.

practice.title: Independent variation
practice.task: Declare const int minutesPerHour=60 and calculate minutes in three hours. Add a comment explaining the number.
criteria: Compare the output with the readable reference case below.
Explain each change using the objects or operations in this topic.
minutesPerHour stays 60 and hours=3 produces 180. Assigning minutesPerHour=30 after its const declaration is invalid; a comment does not change its value.
practice.hint: Changing the comment leaves output at 14. Three whole weeks are 7×3=21 days.

steps.action: Declare const int minutesPerHour=60 and calculate minutes in three hours. Add a comment explaining the number.
Write your solution in a separate starter; keep your previous work.
Compare actual output with your prediction and explain any difference.

terms.definition: A value written directly in source: 60, 0b1010, 'A', or "done".
For the simple objects in this lesson, prevents changing the value after initialization by ordinary assignment.
In our integer constant declaration, requires a valid constant-expression initializer and makes the object const.
A source explanation rather than an executable statement; it must stay accurate when code changes.
A literal whose purpose or unit is unclear where it is used. Not every literal is automatically bad.
A notation for a special character within a literal, such as \n for newline or \\ for a backslash.
